records.source: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְאַחַ֤ת שָׁנָה֙ צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ בְמָלְכ֔וֹ וְאַחַ֤ת עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירֽוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ חֲמוּטַ֥ל בַּֽת־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ מִלִּבְנָֽה׃
records.gloss: [A] son of twenty and one year[s] [was] Zedekiah when he became king, and one [and] ten year[s] he reigned in Jerusalem, and [the] name of his mother [was] Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
pieces: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother's name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.

L.1: A son of twenty-one years [was] Zedekiah when he became king, and eleven years he reigned in Jerusalem, and the name of his mother [was] Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.

R.1: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.

decisions.choice: a closing appendix: after "thus far the words of Jeremiah" (51:64), the fall of Jerusalem is told again in prose
decisions.reason: The book's last oracle ends with the note "Thus far the words of Jeremiah" (51:64). What follows is not one of his messages but a prose account of what happened to the city, the temple, the king and the people, so that the book closes by showing his warnings fulfilled. Jeremiah himself is not mentioned in the chapter. The account follows 2 Kings 24:18-25:30 almost verse for verse, and verses 4-16 are also told more briefly in 39:1-10. It leaves out the story of Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:22-26), which the book has already told at length (40:7-41:18), and adds a list of the numbers taken into exile (verses 28-30).

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 24:18
decisions.reason: The Hebrew of this verse is the same as 2 Kings 24:18, so the wording here is the same. 2 Chronicles 36:11 gives the same age and length of reign but leaves out his mother.

decisions.choice: Hamutal: the form read aloud
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 24:18, the written consonants spell the name Hamital; the scribes marked Hamutal to be read aloud, the form used in 2 Kings 23:31. It is the same woman.

decisions.choice: Jeremiah from Libnah: a different man from the prophet
decisions.reason: Hamutal's father shares the prophet's name but is another man. The prophet came from Anathoth, a town of priests in Benjamin (1:1); this Jeremiah came from Libnah, a town in the lowland of Judah. Hamutal was also the mother of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:31), so Zedekiah was Jehoahaz's full brother and a half brother of Jehoiakim.

decisions.choice: eleven years: from 597 BC to the fall of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Nebuchadrezzar made Zedekiah king when he took Jehoiachin to Babylon (2 Kings 24:17), and Zedekiah reigned until the city fell in his eleventh year (verse 5), about 586 BC.

decisions.choice: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 24:18: Balanced and Readable give the age as English does and put the name first. Balanced says "ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years", as Readable does.

records.heading: Jerusalem falls to Babylon

records.source: וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הָרַ֖ע בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה כְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֖ה יְהוֹיָקִֽים׃
records.gloss: And he did the evil in [the] eyes of Yahweh, according to all that had done Jehoiakim.
pieces: He did what was evil in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, as Jehoiakim had done.

L.2: And he did the evil in [the] eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.

R.2: He did what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said was evil, just as Jehoiakim had done.

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 24:19
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is the same as 2 Kings 24:19, and the wording follows it. Zedekiah is measured against his brother Jehoiakim, the king who burned Jeremiah's scroll (36:20-26), not against his father Josiah. The book has shown Zedekiah asking for the LORD's word and then not heeding it (37:17; 38:14-23).

decisions.choice: verses 2-3 are part of the Hebrew text; the Greek lacks them
alternatives: leave out verses 2-3 with the Greek
decisions.reason: As far as is known from general knowledge, the Septuagint of Jeremiah does not have verses 2-3, the verdict on Zedekiah's reign, and goes from his mother's name to the siege. This translation follows the Hebrew (see the note at 1:1).

decisions.choice: the verdict formula
decisions.reason: The verdict on a king keeps the wording set for the books of Kings at each level: "did the evil in [the] eyes of", "did what was evil in the sight of", "did what the LORD said was evil". Balanced says "as Jehoiakim had done" for "according to all that Jehoiakim had done".

records.source: כִּ֣י׀עַל־אַ֣ף יְהוָ֗ה הָֽיְתָה֙ בִּירוּשָׁלִַ֣ם וִֽיהוּדָ֔ה עַד־הִשְׁלִיכ֥וֹ אוֹתָ֖ם מֵעַ֣ל פָּנָ֑יו וַיִּמְרֹ֥ד צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ בְּמֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶֽל׃
records.gloss: For on [the] anger of Yahweh it happened in Jerusalem and in Judah, until he cast them from on his face; and rebelled Zedekiah against [the] king of Babylon.
pieces: It was because of the anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that all this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cast them out of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

L.3: For because of the anger of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} it came to be in Jerusalem and in Judah, until {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cast them out from before {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} face. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

R.3: All this happened to Jerusalem and Judah because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was angry with them, until at last {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} threw them out of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} presence. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

decisions.choice: because of Yahweh's anger it came to be: the events of Zedekiah's reign happened through Yahweh's anger
alternatives: Yahweh's anger was against Jerusalem and Judah
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 24:20, the verb has no stated subject. The sentence means that what happened in Jerusalem and Judah, the evil of its kings and the disaster that followed, came about through Yahweh's anger. It may also be read "Yahweh's anger came upon Jerusalem and Judah"; the sense is close.

decisions.choice: cast them out from before his face: sent them into exile out of his presence
decisions.reason: To be put away from Yahweh's face is to lose the land where he had made his presence known. Jeremiah had used the same words: "I will cast you out from before my face" (7:15).

decisions.choice: Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon: the same words as 2 Kings 24:20
decisions.reason: The whole verse is the same as 2 Kings 24:20. Jeremiah had urged Zedekiah again and again to submit to the king of Babylon and live (27:12-15; 38:17-18). 2 Chronicles 36:13 adds that Nebuchadnezzar had made him swear by God, and Ezekiel 17:13-15 calls the rebellion the breaking of a covenant oath.

decisions.choice: all this
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 24:20, Balanced and Readable supply "all this" for the verb with no stated subject. Readable turns "the anger of the LORD" into "the LORD was angry with them" and adds "at last" for "until".

records.source: וַיְהִי֩ בַשָּׁנָ֨ה הַתְּשִׁעִ֜ית לְמָלְכ֗וֹ בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הָעֲשִׂירִי֮ בֶּעָשׂ֣וֹר לַחֹדֶשׁ֒ בָּ֠א נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֨ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֜ל ה֤וּא וְכָל־חֵילוֹ֙ עַל־יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ עָלֶ֑יהָ וַיִּבְנ֥וּ עָלֶ֛יהָ דָּיֵ֖ק סָבִֽיב׃
records.gloss: And it was in the year the ninth of his reigning, in the month the tenth, on [the] tenth of the month, came Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and they encamped against it, and they built against it siege-work all around.
pieces: On the tenth day of the tenth month, in the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon advanced on Jerusalem with his whole army. They camped against the city and built siege works against it on every side.

L.4: And it came about in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth [day] of the month, [that] Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and they encamped against it; and they built a siege wall against it all around.

R.4: In the ninth year that Zedekiah was king, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadrezzar, the king of Babylon, marched against Jerusalem with his whole army. They set up camp around the city and built ramps and walls against it on every side.

decisions.choice: his reign: the reign of Zedekiah
decisions.reason: The last king named is Zedekiah, who rebelled (verse 3). The siege is dated by the years of his reign.

decisions.choice: the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year: early in 588 BC
decisions.reason: Months are counted from the spring, so the tenth month falls in midwinter. Depending on how the reign years were counted, the siege began early in 588 BC or a year earlier. Ezekiel was told to write down this same day (Ezekiel 24:1-2), and a fast of the tenth month was later kept in memory of it (Zechariah 8:19).

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar: the same king as Nebuchadnezzar
decisions.reason: Jeremiah's Hebrew mostly spells the name Nebuchadrezzar, nearer to the Babylonian Nabu-kudurri-usur; Kings uses Nebuchadnezzar. Each verse keeps the form its Hebrew has (as 39:1 does); it is one king.

decisions.choice: siege works: a wall, ramps or towers built around a besieged city
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:1, the word is used only of siege works (Ezekiel 4:2). It may mean a wall that shut the city in or the ramps and towers built against its walls; either way the city was cut off.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:1 with two small differences
decisions.reason: The verse matches 2 Kings 25:1, but Kings spells the name Nebuchadnezzar and has "he encamped" where Jeremiah has "they encamped", the king and his army. Jeremiah 39:1 gives only the year and the month.

decisions.choice: Zedekiah (Balanced and Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:1, Balanced and Readable name Zedekiah for "his". Readable describes the siege works as ramps and walls.

records.source: וַתָּבֹ֥א הָעִ֖יר בַּמָּצ֑וֹר עַ֚ד עַשְׁתֵּ֣י עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ צִדְקִיָּֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And came the city into the siege until [the] eleventh year of the king Zedekiah.
pieces: The city was under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.

L.5: And the city came into the siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.

R.5: The city was surrounded and cut off until Zedekiah's eleventh year as king.

decisions.choice: came into the siege: was besieged
decisions.reason: The city "came into" a state of siege and stayed in it: no one could go in or out, and no food could be brought in.

decisions.choice: until the eleventh year: about a year and a half
decisions.reason: From the tenth month of the ninth year (verse 4) to the fourth month of the eleventh year (verse 6) is about eighteen months. The siege was broken off for a time when an Egyptian army came out, but the Babylonians returned, as Jeremiah had said they would (37:5-11).

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 25:2
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is the same as 2 Kings 25:2. Jeremiah 39:2 joins this verse to the next and gives the full date of the breach.

decisions.choice: surrounded and cut off (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a siege is instead of using the word.

records.source: בַּחֹ֤דֶשׁ הָֽרְבִיעִי֙ בְּתִשְׁעָ֣ה לַחֹ֔דֶשׁ וַיֶּחֱזַ֥ק הָרָעָ֖ב בָּעִ֑יר וְלֹא־הָיָ֥ה לֶ֖חֶם לְעַ֥ם הָאָֽרֶץ׃
records.gloss: In the month the fourth, on [the] ninth of the month, and was severe the famine in the city, and there was no bread for [the] people of the land.
pieces: By the ninth day of the fourth month the city was gripped by famine, and the people of the land had no food.

L.6: In the fourth month, on the ninth [day] of the month, the famine was severe in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land.

R.6: By the ninth day of the fourth month, there was a terrible famine in the city. The people had nothing left to eat.

decisions.choice: the fourth month named here; 2 Kings 25:3 lacks it
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:3 says only "on the ninth of the month"; Jeremiah names the month, as 39:2 does. Otherwise the verse is the same as Kings, and the wording follows it.

decisions.choice: the ninth day of the fourth month: midsummer, about 586 BC
decisions.reason: The fourth month falls in midsummer. A fast of the fourth month was later kept for the day the city was broken into (Zechariah 8:19).

decisions.choice: bread: food of any kind
decisions.reason: "Bread" often stands for food in general. Jeremiah had been given a daily loaf in the guardhouse "until all the bread in the city was gone" (37:21), and Lamentations 4:4-10 describes the famine.

decisions.choice: the people of the land: the ordinary people shut up in the city
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:3, the phrase here seems to mean the whole common population, including the country people who had fled inside the walls (35:11).

decisions.choice: By the ninth day (Balanced and Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:3, Balanced and Readable say "by" this date, since the famine had been growing and reached its worst then. Readable says "the people" for "the people of the land".

records.source: וַתִּבָּקַ֣ע הָעִ֗יר וְכָל־אַנְשֵׁ֣י הַמִּלְחָמָ֡ה יִבְרְחוּ֩ וַיֵּצְא֨וּ מֵהָעִ֜יר לַ֗יְלָה דֶּ֜רֶךְ שַׁ֤עַר בֵּין־הַחֹמֹתַ֨יִם֙ אֲשֶׁר֙ עַל־גַּ֣ן הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְכַשְׂדִּ֥ים עַל־הָעִ֖יר סָבִ֑יב וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ דֶּ֥רֶךְ הָעֲרָבָֽה׃
records.gloss: And was broken into the city, and all [the] men of the war fled and went out from the city [by] night [by the] way of [the] gate between the two walls which [was] by [the] garden of the king, and [the] Chaldeans [were] against the city all around; and they went [the] way of the Arabah.
pieces: Then the city wall was breached, and all the soldiers fled. They left the city by night through the gate between the two walls near the king's garden, though the Chaldeans were all around the city, and they went off toward the Arabah.

L.7: And the city was broken into, and all the men of war fled and went out of the city by night by way of the gate between the two walls, which [was] by the king's garden, while the Chaldeans [were] against the city all around; and they went by way of the Arabah.

R.7: Then the enemy broke through the city wall. All the soldiers ran away. That night they escaped from the city through the gate between the two walls near the king's garden, even though the Babylonians were all around the city. They fled toward the Jordan Valley.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:4 with the verbs filled in
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:4 has no verb for the soldiers and says "he went" toward the Arabah. Jeremiah says they "fled and went out of the city" and "they went", the king and the soldiers with him (verse 8). Jeremiah 39:4 adds that Zedekiah and the soldiers fled when they saw the Babylonian officers sitting in the gate.

decisions.choice: the gate between the two walls by the king's garden: at the south end of the city
decisions.reason: The king's garden lay at the south end of Jerusalem near the Pool of Siloam (Nehemiah 3:15). A gate there between two lines of wall led down into the valley, away from the main Babylonian lines.

decisions.choice: the Chaldeans: the Babylonians
decisions.reason: The Chaldeans were a people of southern Mesopotamia. Nebuchadrezzar's family was Chaldean, so the name came to mean the Babylonians and their army.

decisions.choice: the Arabah: the Jordan Valley
decisions.reason: The Arabah is the deep valley of the Jordan running down to the Dead Sea. They were making for the river crossings near Jericho (verse 8), perhaps to reach Ammon on the far side.

decisions.choice: the city wall (Balanced and Readable); the enemy (Readable)
decisions.reason: "The city was broken into" means that a breach was made in its wall; Balanced and Readable say so, and Readable names who made it.

decisions.choice: the Babylonians; the Jordan Valley (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable uses the better-known name "Babylonians" for the Chaldeans throughout the chapter and explains the Arabah as the Jordan Valley.

records.source: וַיִּרְדְּפ֤וּ חֵיל־כַּשְׂדִּים֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיַּשִּׂ֥יגוּ אֶת־צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ בְּעַֽרְבֹ֣ת יְרֵח֑וֹ וְכָל־חֵיל֔וֹ נָפֹ֖צוּ מֵעָלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And pursued [the] army of [the] Chaldeans after the king, and overtook Zedekiah in [the] plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.
pieces: But the Chaldean army chased the king and caught up with Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army scattered away from him.

L.8: And the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king, and they overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.

R.8: But the Babylonian army chased after the king and caught up with Zedekiah on the plains near Jericho. All his soldiers scattered and left him.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:5, with Zedekiah named
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as 2 Kings 25:5, except that Kings says "overtook him" and Jeremiah names Zedekiah. Jeremiah 39:5 joins it to the next verse.

decisions.choice: the plains of Jericho: the flat valley floor near the Jordan
decisions.reason: Jericho lies in the Jordan Valley some fifteen miles east of Jerusalem and far below it. Zedekiah had almost reached the river.

decisions.choice: his army was scattered from him: they ran off and left him alone
decisions.reason: The soldiers who had fled with him scattered, so the king was taken with no one to defend him.

decisions.choice: Babylonian (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 7.

records.source: וַֽיִּתְפְּשׂוּ֙ אֶת־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיַּעֲל֨וּ אֹת֜וֹ אֶל־מֶ֧לֶךְ בָּבֶ֛ל רִבְלָ֖תָה בְּאֶ֣רֶץ חֲמָ֑ת וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ מִשְׁפָּטִֽים׃
records.gloss: And they seized the king, and brought him up to [the] king of Babylon to Riblah in [the] land of Hamath, and he spoke with him judgments.
pieces: They seized the king and took him up to Riblah in the land of Hamath, to the king of Babylon, and there the king passed sentence on him.

L.9: And they seized the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he spoke judgments with him.

R.9: They captured King Zedekiah and took him to the king of Babylon at the town of Riblah in the land of Hamath. There the king of Babylon put him on trial and sentenced him.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:6 with "in the land of Hamath" and "he spoke judgments"
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:6 does not name Hamath and says "they spoke judgment with him". Jeremiah has the singular verb, the king of Babylon himself, and the plural "judgments", the charges and the sentence. Jeremiah 39:5 has the same words as this verse.

decisions.choice: Riblah in the land of Hamath: a town far to the north, in Syria
decisions.reason: Riblah stood on the Orontes River in the territory of Hamath. Nebuchadrezzar directed his campaign from there, as Pharaoh Neco had held King Jehoahaz there (2 Kings 23:33).

decisions.choice: spoke judgments with him: tried him and passed sentence
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of bringing a legal case against someone (1:16; 4:12). Zedekiah was judged as a vassal who had broken his oath of loyalty (verse 3).

decisions.choice: the king (Balanced); the king of Babylon, King Zedekiah, put on trial and sentenced (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say who "he" is, and Readable names Zedekiah and spells out the legal sense of the idiom.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁחַ֧ט מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֛ל אֶת־בְּנֵ֥י צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ לְעֵינָ֑יו וְגַ֛ם אֶת־כָּל־שָׂרֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה שָׁחַ֥ט בְּרִבְלָֽתָה׃
records.gloss: And slaughtered [the] king of Babylon [the] sons of Zedekiah before his eyes; and also all [the] princes of Judah he slaughtered at Riblah.
pieces: The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah's sons while he watched, and he also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah.

L.10: And the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes; and also all the princes of Judah he slaughtered at Riblah.

R.10: The king of Babylon killed Zedekiah's sons while Zedekiah watched. He also killed all the leaders of Judah there at Riblah.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:7 names no killer and no officials
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:7 says "they slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes". Jeremiah names the king of Babylon as the one who did it and adds that he also killed all the officials of Judah at Riblah. Jeremiah 39:6 has the same addition with a different word, "nobles".

decisions.choice: the princes of Judah: the king's officials
decisions.reason: The word names the officials who held office under the king. Some of them had demanded Jeremiah's death and had him thrown into the cistern (38:4-6, 25-27); now they died with the king's sons.

decisions.choice: the sons killed before his eyes
decisions.reason: Killing a rebel king's sons ended his line; the last thing Zedekiah saw was their death (verse 11).

decisions.choice: princes (Literal); officials (Balanced); leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word for royal officials keeps the wording set for these books at each level. Readable says "while Zedekiah watched" so that "he" is clear.

records.source: וְאֶת־עֵינֵ֥י צִדְקִיָּ֖הוּ עִוֵּ֑ר וַיַּאַסְרֵ֣הוּ בַֽנְחֻשְׁתַּ֗יִם וַיְבִאֵ֤הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶל֙ בָּבֶ֔לָה וַיִּתְּנֵ֥הוּ בֵֽית־הַפְּקֻדֹּ֖ת עַד־י֥וֹם מוֹתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And [the] eyes of Zedekiah he blinded, and bound him with bronze fetters, and brought him [the] king of Babylon to Babylon, and put him [in the] house of the custodies until [the] day of his death.
pieces: Then he put out Zedekiah's eyes and bound him in bronze fetters, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon and kept him in prison until the day he died.

L.11: And he put out the eyes of Zedekiah and bound him in bronze fetters, and the king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in the house of custody until the day of his death.

R.11: Then he had Zedekiah's eyes put out. He had him bound in bronze chains, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon. He kept him in prison there until the day Zedekiah died.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:7 ends at Babylon; Jeremiah adds the prison until his death
decisions.reason: The first part follows 2 Kings 25:7, with "the king of Babylon" named. Kings ends with "brought him to Babylon"; Jeremiah adds that he was put in prison there until the day of his death. Jeremiah 39:7 also ends at Babylon.

decisions.choice: the house of custody: a prison
decisions.reason: The word comes from a verb meaning to oversee or to punish, and the phrase names a place where prisoners were kept under guard. It is used of a prison only here.

decisions.choice: the prophets' words come true
decisions.reason: Jeremiah had told Zedekiah that he would see the king of Babylon face to face and go to Babylon (32:4-5; 34:3), and Ezekiel had said that the prince would be brought to Babylon "but he will not see it, and there he will die" (Ezekiel 12:13).

decisions.choice: bronze fetters: a pair of bronze shackles
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:7, the word is "bronze" in the dual form, a pair of bronze shackles (Judges 16:21).

decisions.choice: had ... put out; had him bound; chains (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:7, Readable says the king "had" these things done, and names Zedekiah again at the end so that "he" is clear.

records.source: וּבַחֹ֤דֶשׁ הַֽחֲמִישִׁי֙ בֶּעָשׂ֣וֹר לַחֹ֔דֶשׁ הִ֗יא שְׁנַת֙ תְּשַֽׁע־עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֣ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֑ל בָּ֗א נְבֽוּזַרְאֲדָן֙ רַב־טַבָּחִ֔ים עָמַ֛ד לִפְנֵ֥י מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֖ל בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: And in the month the fifth, on [the] tenth of the month, it [was the] year nineteen year of the king Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards, [who] stood before [the] king of Babylon, into Jerusalem.
pieces: In the fifth month, on the tenth day, the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadrezzar's reign over Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, who served the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.

L.12: And in the fifth month, on the tenth [day] of the month, which [was] the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard, [who] stood before the king of Babylon, came into Jerusalem.

R.12: On the tenth day of the fifth month, Nebuzaradan came to Jerusalem. He was the commander of the royal guard and served the king of Babylon at his court. This was in the nineteenth year that Nebuchadrezzar was king of Babylon.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:8: the seventh day, and "servant of the king of Babylon"
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:8 dates Nebuzaradan's arrival to the seventh of the month, not the tenth, calls him "servant of the king of Babylon" instead of one "who stood before the king of Babylon", and spells the king's name Nebuchadnezzar. The two dates may count his setting out and his arrival, or one number may have been miscopied. Jeremiah 39:9 gives no date. The Hebrew of each book is followed.

decisions.choice: chief of the guard: literally "chief of the slaughterers"
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:8, the word for the guards first meant butchers or cooks, but in a royal title it names the king's bodyguard, who also carried out executions (Genesis 37:36). Here it is the title of a senior Babylonian officer.

decisions.choice: stood before the king of Babylon: served him as a court officer
decisions.reason: To "stand before" a king is to wait on him as one of his officers (1 Kings 10:8; 12:8). It says the same as "servant" in 2 Kings 25:8: Nebuzaradan was one of Nebuchadrezzar's own officials.

decisions.choice: the fifth month of Nebuchadrezzar's nineteenth year: midsummer 586 BC
decisions.reason: Nebuchadrezzar's nineteenth year is Zedekiah's eleventh (verse 5). The burning of the temple came about a month after the city fell, and "the fast of the fifth month" was later kept in mourning for it (Zechariah 7:3, 5; 8:19). Verse 29 dates the deportation from Jerusalem to the king's eighteenth year; see the note there.

decisions.choice: who served the king of Babylon (Balanced); served the king of Babylon at his court (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom "stood before" instead of the picture.

decisions.choice: chief of the guard (Literal); captain of the guard (Balanced); commander of the royal guard (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25, each level keeps its own wording for the title throughout the chapter. Readable moves the date by the king's reign to the end so that the sentence about Nebuzaradan stays short.

records.source: וַיִּשְׂרֹ֥ף אֶת־בֵּית־יְהוָ֖ה וְאֶת־בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְאֵ֨ת כָּל־בָּתֵּ֧י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֛ם וְאֶת־כָּל־בֵּ֥ית הַגָּד֖וֹל שָׂרַ֥ף בָּאֵֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And he burned [the] house of Yahweh and [the] house of the king, and all [the] houses of Jerusalem; and every house of the great [one] he burned with fire.
pieces: He burned the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the king's palace and all the houses of Jerusalem; every important house he burned down.

L.13: And he burned the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and the house of the king and all the houses of Jerusalem; and every great house he burned with fire.

R.13: He set fire to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple, the royal palace and all the houses in Jerusalem. He burned down every important building.

decisions.choice: the house of the LORD burned, as Jeremiah had warned
decisions.reason: Solomon's temple had stood for nearly four hundred years. In his temple sermon Jeremiah had warned that the LORD would do to this house what he had done to Shiloh (7:12-14; 26:6), and for saying it he was nearly put to death (26:8-9).

decisions.choice: every great house: the houses of the important people
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:9, the Hebrew can mean every large building or the house of every "great one", the leading men of the city. Either way it points to the main buildings of Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 25:9
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as 2 Kings 25:9, except that Jeremiah puts "the" with "great". Jeremiah 39:8 does not name the temple; it says the Chaldeans burned the king's house and "the house of the people".

decisions.choice: the king's palace; temple (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:9, "the house of the king" is the palace at Balanced and Readable, and Readable says "temple" for the house of the LORD.

records.source: וְאֶת־כָּל־חֹמ֥וֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם סָבִ֑יב נָֽתְצוּ֙ כָּל־חֵ֣יל כַּשְׂדִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֖ר אֶת־רַב־טַבָּחִֽים׃
records.gloss: And all [the] walls of Jerusalem all around broke down all [the] army of [the] Chaldeans who [were] with [the] chief of [the] guards.
pieces: The whole Chaldean army that was with the captain of the guard tore down all the walls around Jerusalem.

L.14: And all the army of the Chaldeans who [were] with the chief of the guard broke down all the walls around Jerusalem.

R.14: The whole Babylonian army that was with the commander of the guard tore down all the walls around Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:10 with "all" and "with"
decisions.reason: The verse follows 2 Kings 25:10. Jeremiah says "all the walls", and has the word "with" ("who were with the chief of the guard") that Kings lacks. Jeremiah 39:8 says simply that the Chaldeans broke down the walls.

decisions.choice: the walls broken down: the city left without defense
decisions.reason: Without walls a city could not protect itself. Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins until Nehemiah rebuilt them (Nehemiah 1:3; 2:17).

decisions.choice: the army ... broke down the walls
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts the walls first and the army last. All three levels put the subject first, as 2 Kings 25:10 does; Readable says "Babylonian" as elsewhere.

records.source: וּמִדַּלּ֨וֹת הָעָ֜ם וְֽאֶת־יֶ֥תֶר הָעָ֣ם׀הַנִּשְׁאָרִ֣ים בָּעִ֗יר וְאֶת־הַנֹּֽפְלִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָֽפְלוּ֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ בָּבֶ֔ל וְאֵ֖ת יֶ֣תֶר הָֽאָמ֑וֹן הֶגְלָ֕ה נְבוּזַרְאֲדָ֖ן רַב־טַבָּחִֽים׃
records.gloss: And from [the] poor ones of the people, and [the] rest of the people who were left in the city, and the deserters who had deserted to [the] king of Babylon, and [the] rest of the craftsmen, exiled Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards.
pieces: Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile some of the poorest of the people, the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen.

L.15: And some of the poorest of the people, and the rest of the people who were left in the city, and the deserters who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen, Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard carried into exile.

R.15: Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took people away as captives. These included some of the poorest people, the rest of the people still left in the city, those who had gone over to the side of the king of Babylon, and the rest of the skilled workers.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:11 with two differences
decisions.reason: The verse follows 2 Kings 25:11, but Jeremiah begins the list with "some of the poorest of the people", and where Kings ends with "the rest of the multitude" Jeremiah has "the rest of the craftsmen". Jeremiah 39:9 repeats "the rest of the people who remained" instead.

decisions.choice: craftsmen: skilled workers
alternatives: the rest of the multitude, as 2 Kings 25:11
decisions.reason: The word differs from the one in 2 Kings 25:11, "multitude", by one letter. It is taken here as "craftsmen" or "master workers" (compare Proverbs 8:30). One of the two may have come from the other in copying; the Hebrew of each book is followed.

decisions.choice: some of the poorest of the people taken, though the poorest of the land were left (verse 16)
alternatives: the words are a copying slip from verse 16
decisions.reason: Some of the poor were taken and some left. "The people" here may be the people of the city, and "the land" in verse 16 the countryside, so that the poor of Jerusalem went into exile while the poor of the farms stayed. It is also possible that the words were carried over in copying from the start of verse 16.

decisions.choice: fallen to the king of Babylon: deserted to him
decisions.reason: To "fall to" an enemy means to go over to his side. Jeremiah had urged the people to do this to save their lives (21:9; 38:2), and Zedekiah feared those who had done so (38:19).

decisions.choice: Nebuzaradan ... carried into exile (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts the groups first and the verb and its subject last. Literal keeps that order; Balanced and Readable start with Nebuzaradan, and Readable lists the groups in a second sentence.

records.source: וּמִדַּלּ֣וֹת הָאָ֔רֶץ הִשְׁאִ֕יר נְבוּזַרְאֲדָ֖ן רַב־טַבָּחִ֑ים לְכֹרְמִ֖ים וּלְיֹגְבִֽים׃
records.gloss: And some of [the] poor of the land left Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards for vinedressers and for field-workers.
pieces: But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest people of the land to tend the vineyards and work the fields.

L.16: But some of the poorest of the land Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard left as vinedressers and as field workers.

R.16: But Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, left behind some of the poorest people in the land. He had them take care of the vineyards and work the fields.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:12, with Nebuzaradan named
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as 2 Kings 25:12 except that it names Nebuzaradan, where Kings has only his title. Jeremiah 39:10 adds that he gave the poor vineyards and fields on that day.

decisions.choice: field workers: probably plowmen or farm laborers
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:12, the word is rare and its exact sense is not known. Beside "vinedressers" it names some kind of work on the land, perhaps plowing or tilling.

decisions.choice: some of the poorest left to work the land
decisions.reason: The land was not left empty. Those who had owned nothing were left to keep the vineyards and fields producing (39:10).

decisions.choice: to tend the vineyards and work the fields (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:12, Balanced and Readable describe the work instead of using the nouns "vinedressers" and "field workers".

records.source: וְאֶת־עַמּוּדֵ֨י הַנְּחֹ֜שֶׁת אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְבֵית־יְהוָ֗ה וְֽאֶת־הַמְּכֹנ֞וֹת וְאֶת־יָ֧ם הַנְּחֹ֛שֶׁת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּבֵית־יְהוָ֖ה שִׁבְּר֣וּ כַשְׂדִּ֑ים וַיִּשְׂא֥וּ אֶת־כָּל־נְחֻשְׁתָּ֖ם בָּבֶֽלָה׃
records.gloss: And [the] pillars of the bronze which [belonged] to [the] house of Yahweh, and the stands, and [the] sea of the bronze which [was] in [the] house of Yahweh, broke in pieces [the] Chaldeans, and carried all their bronze to Babylon.
pieces: The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars that belonged to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the stands, and the bronze Sea that was in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and they hauled all the metal off to Babylon.

L.17: And the pillars of bronze that [belonged] to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and the stands and the sea of bronze that [was] in the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the Chaldeans broke in pieces, and they carried all their bronze to Babylon.

R.17: The Babylonians broke into pieces the bronze pillars of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple, the bronze stands on wheels, and the huge bronze tank called the Sea. They carried all the bronze away to Babylon.

decisions.choice: the pillars, the stands and the Sea that Solomon had made
decisions.reason: These are the great bronze works cast for Solomon's temple: the two pillars at the porch (1 Kings 7:15-22), the great basin called the Sea (1 Kings 7:23-26), and the ten wheeled stands for basins of water (1 Kings 7:27-37).

decisions.choice: broken in pieces and the bronze carried off, as Jeremiah had said
decisions.reason: The pieces were too large to carry whole, so they were broken up for their metal. When other prophets promised that the temple vessels would soon come back, Jeremiah said that the pillars, the Sea and the stands still left would be carried to Babylon too (27:16-22).

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:13 with "belonged to" and "all"
decisions.reason: The verse follows 2 Kings 25:13. Jeremiah says the pillars "belonged to" the house of the LORD where Kings says they were "in" it, and "all their bronze" where Kings says "their bronze".

decisions.choice: the Sea; stands on wheels, a huge bronze tank called the Sea (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:13, Balanced writes "the Sea" as a name, and Readable says what the stands and the Sea were. Readable says "temple" for the house of the LORD and mentions it once.

records.source: וְאֶת־הַ֠סִּרוֹת וְאֶת־הַיָּעִ֨ים וְאֶת־הַֽמְזַמְּר֜וֹת וְאֶת־הַמִּזְרָקֹ֣ת וְאֶת־הַכַּפּ֗וֹת וְאֵ֨ת כָּל־כְּלֵ֧י הַנְּחֹ֛שֶׁת אֲשֶׁר־יְשָׁרְת֥וּ בָהֶ֖ם לָקָֽחוּ׃
records.gloss: And the pots and the shovels and the snuffers and the bowls and the dishes and all [the] vessels of the bronze which they served with them, they took.
pieces: They also took away the pots, the shovels, the wick trimmers, the sprinkling bowls, the dishes and all the bronze utensils used in the temple service.

L.18: And the pots and the shovels and the snuffers and the bowls and the dishes and all the vessels of bronze with which they served, they took away.

R.18: They also took the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls and dishes, and all the other bronze things used in the worship at the temple.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:14 with the bowls added
decisions.reason: The list is the same as in 2 Kings 25:14 with "the bowls" added after the snuffers. Kings names the bowls in the next verse, with the firepans.

decisions.choice: pots, shovels, snuffers, bowls, dishes: tools for the altar, the lamps and the incense
decisions.reason: The pots carried away ashes and the shovels served the altar (1 Kings 7:40, 45); the snuffers trimmed the lamp wicks, and the bowls were used to sprinkle the blood of the offerings (1 Kings 7:50; Exodus 27:3); the dishes held incense (Numbers 7:14).

decisions.choice: served: the priests' ministry in the temple
decisions.reason: The verb is used of the priests' service at the altar and in the sanctuary (Exodus 28:43; Numbers 4:12).

decisions.choice: snuffers, bowls (Literal); wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1 Kings 7:50 and 2 Kings 25:14-15. Balanced and Readable say "in the temple service" and "in the worship at the temple" for "with which they served".

records.source: וְאֶת־הַ֠סִּפִּים וְאֶת־הַמַּחְתּ֨וֹת וְאֶת־הַמִּזְרָק֜וֹת וְאֶת־הַסִּיר֣וֹת וְאֶת־הַמְּנֹר֗וֹת וְאֶת־הַכַּפּוֹת֙ וְאֶת־הַמְּנַקִי֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֤ר זָהָב֙ זָהָ֔ב וַאֲשֶׁר־כֶּ֖סֶף כָּ֑סֶף לָקַ֖ח רַב־טַבָּחִֽים׃
records.gloss: And the cups and the firepans and the bowls and the pots and the lampstands and the dishes and the jugs, which [were] gold [as] gold, and which [were] silver [as] silver, took [the] chief of [the] guards.
pieces: The captain of the guard took away the cups, the firepans, the sprinkling bowls, the pots, the lampstands, the dishes and the jars for drink offerings, everything that was made of gold and everything that was made of silver.

L.19: And the cups and the firepans and the bowls and the pots and the lampstands and the dishes and the jugs, what [was] gold, gold, and what [was] silver, silver, the chief of the guard took away.

R.19: The commander of the guard also took the cups, fire pans, sprinkling bowls, pots, lampstands, dishes and the jars used for drink offerings. He took everything made of gold and everything made of silver.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:15 with a longer list
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:15 names only the firepans and the bowls. Jeremiah adds the cups, pots, lampstands, dishes and jugs, much as 1 Kings 7:49-50 lists the gold furnishings Solomon made.

decisions.choice: gold, gold; silver, silver: everything of gold and everything of silver
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:15, the doubled word gathers everything of that metal: whatever was gold and whatever was silver. Some take it to stress the metal, "pure gold", or to mean that these were taken for their value as metal.

decisions.choice: jugs: vessels for pouring drink offerings
decisions.reason: The word is used of the jugs on the table of the bread of the presence, "with which drink offerings are poured out" (Exodus 25:29; Numbers 4:7).

decisions.choice: lampstands: the ten lampstands of Solomon's temple
decisions.reason: Solomon had made ten gold lampstands for the temple, five on each side (1 Kings 7:49).

decisions.choice: firepans, fire pans (Readable); sprinkling bowls; jars for drink offerings (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1 Kings 7:50, 2 Kings 25:15 and Exodus 25:29. Balanced and Readable add what the jars were for.

records.source: הָעַמּוּדִ֣ים׀שְׁנַ֗יִם הַיָּ֤ם אֶחָד֙ וְהַבָּקָ֞ר שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂ֤ר נְחֹ֨שֶׁת֙ אֲשֶׁר־תַּ֣חַת הַמְּכֹנ֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֛ה הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה לְבֵ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה לֹא־הָיָ֣ה מִשְׁקָ֔ל לִנְחֻשְׁתָּ֖ם כָּל־הַכֵּלִ֥ים הָאֵֽלֶּה׃
records.gloss: The pillars two, the sea one, and the bulls twelve [of] bronze which [were] under the stands, which had made the king Solomon for [the] house of Yahweh, there was no weight to their bronze, all the vessels these.
pieces: As for the two pillars, the one Sea and the twelve bronze bulls under the stands, which King Solomon made for the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the bronze of all these things was more than could be weighed.

L.20: The two pillars, the one sea, and the twelve bulls of bronze that [were] under the stands, which King Solomon had made for the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: there was no weight for the bronze of all these vessels.

R.20: The two pillars, the Sea, and the twelve bronze bulls under the stands, all made by King Solomon for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s temple, held so much bronze that no one could weigh it.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:16 with the twelve bronze bulls added
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:16 names the two pillars, the Sea and the stands. Jeremiah adds the twelve bronze bulls and says "King Solomon". The bulls held up the Sea (1 Kings 7:25). Kings says that King Ahaz had taken the Sea down from the bulls and set it on a stone base (2 Kings 16:17), which may be why Kings does not name them here.

decisions.choice: under the stands: the Hebrew as it stands
alternatives: the twelve bronze bulls that were under the Sea
the twelve bronze bulls that were underneath, and the stands
decisions.reason: The bulls stood under the Sea, not under the stands (1 Kings 7:25). The Hebrew may mean "the bulls that were underneath, and the stands", with the stands listed separately as in 2 Kings 25:16, or a word may have been lost. As far as is known from general knowledge, the Greek reads "under the sea". The Hebrew wording is kept.

decisions.choice: there was no weight: it was too much to weigh
decisions.reason: The words repeat 1 Kings 7:47, where Solomon left the bronze unweighed because there was so much of it. What was too great to weigh when the temple was built is now carried away.

decisions.choice: all made by King Solomon (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Which King Solomon had made" most likely covers everything listed, not only the stands; Readable says "all made by" to show it. Readable leaves out "one" with the Sea.

records.source: וְהָעַמּוּדִ֗ים שְׁמֹנֶ֨ה עֶשְׂרֵ֤ה אַמָּה֙ קוֹמַת֙ הָעַמֻּ֣ד הָאֶחָ֔ד וְח֛וּט שְׁתֵּים־עֶשְׂרֵ֥ה אַמָּ֖ה יְסֻבֶּ֑נּוּ וְעָבְי֛וֹ אַרְבַּ֥ע אַצְבָּע֖וֹת נָבֽוּב׃
records.gloss: And the pillars, eighteen cubit[s] [was the] height of the pillar the one, and a line of twelve cubit[s] went around it, and its thickness [was] four fingers, hollow.
pieces: As for the pillars, each pillar was {{units:about 27 feet|eighteen cubits}} high, and it took a line of {{units:about 18 feet|twelve cubits}} to go around it. Its metal was {{units:about 3 inches|four fingers}} thick, and it was hollow.

L.21: And the pillars: eighteen cubits [was] the height of the one pillar, and a line of twelve cubits went around it, and its thickness [was] four fingers; [it was] hollow.

R.21: Each pillar was {{units:about 27 feet|eighteen cubits}} tall and {{units:about 18 feet|twelve cubits}} around. It was hollow, and its bronze was {{units:about 3 inches|four fingers}} thick.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:17 and 1 Kings 7:15
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:17 gives only the height, eighteen cubits. Jeremiah adds the measure around, twelve cubits, as 1 Kings 7:15 has it, and the thickness of the metal and that the pillars were hollow, which no other passage says.

decisions.choice: the height of the one pillar: of each pillar
decisions.reason: "The one pillar" means each of the two; the next verse says the second was like it (1 Kings 7:15).

decisions.choice: four fingers: about three inches
decisions.reason: A finger's breadth was the smallest measure of length, a quarter of a handbreadth. The pillars were cast as hollow bronze columns with walls about three inches thick.

decisions.choice: modern measures with the cubits and fingers as the alternative (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1 Kings 7:15, a cubit is about 18 inches; four fingers are about 3 inches. Literal keeps the Hebrew units. Readable puts "hollow" before the thickness so the sentence reads more easily.

records.source: וְכֹתֶ֨רֶת עָלָ֜יו נְחֹ֗שֶׁת וְקוֹמַ֨ת הַכֹּתֶ֥רֶת הָאַחַת֮ חָמֵ֣שׁ אַמּוֹת֒ וּשְׂבָכָ֨ה וְרִמּוֹנִ֧ים עַֽל־הַכּוֹתֶ֛רֶת סָבִ֖יב הַכֹּ֣ל נְחֹ֑שֶׁת וְכָאֵ֛לֶּה לַֽעַמּ֥וּד הַשֵּׁנִ֖י וְרִמּוֹנִֽים׃

pieces: On top of it was a bronze capital. The capital was {{units:about 7 1/2 feet|five cubits}} high, with a network and pomegranates all around it, all of bronze. The second pillar, with its pomegranates, was the same.

L.22: And on it [was] a capital of bronze; and the height of the one capital [was] five cubits, and a network and pomegranates [were] on the capital all around, all of bronze; and the second pillar [had] the like, and pomegranates.

R.22: It had a bronze top, called a capital, that was {{units:about 7 1/2 feet|five cubits}} tall. All around the capital was a net of lattice work with pomegranates on it, all made of bronze. The second pillar, with its pomegranates, was just the same.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:17: three cubits there, five here
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 25:17 gives the capital a height of three cubits; Jeremiah gives five, as 1 Kings 7:16 and 2 Chronicles 3:15 do. Kings may have a copying error, or may measure only part of the capital. Kings also ends "with the network", where Jeremiah ends "and pomegranates".

decisions.choice: network and pomegranates: a lattice with bronze fruit
decisions.reason: As in 1 Kings 7:17-20, the network is a lattice of crossing bands around the capital, and the pomegranates are bronze ornaments in rows on it.

decisions.choice: like these to the second pillar: the second was the same
decisions.reason: Everything said of the first pillar holds for the second; "and pomegranates" names the part described most fully in the next verse.

decisions.choice: a bronze top, called a capital (Readable); modern measure (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:17, Readable explains "capital"; five cubits are about 7 1/2 feet, as in 1 Kings 7:16.

records.source: וַיִּֽהְיוּ֙ הָֽרִמֹּנִ֔ים תִּשְׁעִ֥ים וְשִׁשָּׁ֖ה ר֑וּחָה כָּל־הָרִמּוֹנִ֥ים מֵאָ֛ה עַל־הַשְּׂבָכָ֖ה סָבִֽיב׃
records.gloss: And were the pomegranates ninety and six toward [the] wind; all the pomegranates [were a] hundred on the network all around.
pieces: There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; in all there were a hundred pomegranates on the network all around.

L.23: And the pomegranates were ninety-six on the sides; all the pomegranates [were] a hundred on the network all around.

R.23: There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides. Altogether a hundred pomegranates went around the network.

decisions.choice: on the sides: literally "toward the wind"
decisions.reason: The phrase, used only here, seems to mean the sides facing outward, toward the four winds. Perhaps ninety-six could be seen from the sides and four more were hidden or stood at the corners, making a hundred in each row. The exact sense is not known.

decisions.choice: a hundred in a row: 1 Kings 7:20, 42
decisions.reason: 1 Kings 7:20 speaks of two hundred pomegranates in rows around each capital, and 1 Kings 7:42 of four hundred for the two networks, two rows on each. That fits a hundred in each row. 2 Kings 25 gives no numbers.

decisions.choice: on the sides
decisions.reason: All levels say "on the sides" for the rare phrase "toward the wind", without settling what it means (see the meaning decision).

records.source: וַיִּקַּ֣ח רַב־טַבָּחִ֗ים אֶת־שְׂרָיָה֙ כֹּהֵ֣ן הָרֹ֔אשׁ וְאֶת־צְפַנְיָ֖ה כֹּהֵ֣ן הַמִּשְׁנֶ֑ה וְאֶת־שְׁלֹ֖שֶׁת שֹׁמְרֵ֥י הַסַּֽף׃
records.gloss: And took [the] chief of [the] guards Seraiah [the] priest of the head, and Zephaniah [the] priest of the second [rank], and [the] three keepers of the threshold.
pieces: The captain of the guard also seized Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest next to him, and the three doorkeepers.

L.24: And the chief of the guard took Seraiah the head priest and Zephaniah the second priest and the three keepers of the threshold.

R.24: The commander of the guard also arrested Seraiah the high priest, Zephaniah the priest next in rank, and the three men who guarded the temple entrance.

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 25:18
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as 2 Kings 25:18 apart from a shorter spelling of Zephaniah's name and "the" before "second", and the wording follows it.

decisions.choice: Seraiah the head priest: the high priest
decisions.reason: "The head priest" is the leading priest of the temple (2 Chronicles 19:11). Seraiah was the grandson of Hilkiah, the high priest under Josiah, and an ancestor of Ezra (1 Chronicles 5:39-41; Ezra 7:1). He is not the Seraiah son of Neriah of 51:59.

decisions.choice: Zephaniah the second priest: the high priest's deputy
decisions.reason: The priest "of second rank" was next after the high priest (2 Kings 23:4). Zephaniah son of Maaseiah carried messages between King Zedekiah and Jeremiah (21:1; 29:25-29; 37:3).

decisions.choice: the keepers of the threshold: senior temple officers
decisions.reason: They guarded the entrances of the temple and received the money brought in (2 Kings 12:10; 22:4). Jeremiah 35:4 names one of them, Maaseiah son of Shallum.

decisions.choice: doorkeepers (Balanced); the men who guarded the temple entrance (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:18, Balanced and Readable explain the titles, and Readable says "arrested" for "took".

records.source: וּמִן־הָעִ֡יר לָקַח֩ סָרִ֨יס אֶחָ֜ד אֲֽשֶׁר־הָיָ֥ה פָקִ֣יד׀עַל־אַנְשֵׁ֣י הַמִּלְחָמָ֗ה וְשִׁבְעָ֨ה אֲנָשִׁ֜ים מֵרֹאֵ֤י פְנֵי־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִמְצְא֣וּ בָעִ֔יר וְאֵ֗ת סֹפֵר֙ שַׂ֣ר הַצָּבָ֔א הַמַּצְבִּ֖א אֶת־עַ֣ם הָאָ֑רֶץ וְשִׁשִּׁ֥ים אִישׁ֙ מֵעַ֣ם הָאָ֔רֶץ הַֽנִּמְצְאִ֖ים בְּת֥וֹךְ הָעִֽיר׃
records.gloss: And from the city he took one official who had been overseer over [the] men of the war, and seven men of [those] seeing [the] face of the king who were found in the city, and [the] scribe of [the] commander of the army, the one mustering the people of the land, and sixty men of [the] people of the land, the ones found in [the] midst of the city.
pieces: From the city he took a court officer who had been in charge of the soldiers, seven of the king's advisers who were found in the city, the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land for war, and sixty of the people of the land who were still in the city.

L.25: And from the city he took one eunuch who had been the overseer over the men of war, and seven men of those who saw the face of the king, who were found in the city, and the scribe of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land, and sixty men of the people of the land who were found in the midst of the city.

R.25: From the city he also took the palace official in charge of the soldiers and seven of the king's close advisers who were still in the city. He took the army commander's secretary, who called up the men of the land to serve in the army. He also took sixty of those men who were still in the city.

decisions.choice: seven of the king's advisers here; five in 2 Kings 25:19
decisions.reason: The verse follows 2 Kings 25:19, but where Kings has five men "who saw the face of the king", Jeremiah has seven. One number may have been miscopied; the Hebrew of each book is followed. Jeremiah also says the officer "had been" in charge, and "in the midst of the city" for "in the city".

decisions.choice: a royal officer
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:19, the word can mean a eunuch, but it was also a title for a high officer of the king (Genesis 37:36). Here it is a military officer in command of the soldiers.

decisions.choice: those who saw the face of the king: his closest advisers
decisions.reason: Only trusted counselors were allowed into the king's presence (Esther 1:14).

decisions.choice: the scribe of the commander of the army
decisions.reason: Jeremiah's Hebrew reads plainly "the scribe of the commander of the army", the secretary who kept the lists for calling men up. 2 Kings 25:19 can be read "the scribe, the commander of the army"; Jeremiah settles the sense.

decisions.choice: the people of the land: the landholding men of Judah
decisions.reason: Here the phrase names the citizens of Judah who held land and were called up to fight (34:19; 2 Kings 23:30). The sixty were probably leading men of that class.

decisions.choice: the king's advisers; mustered ... for war (Balanced); called up ... to serve in the army (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:19, Balanced and Readable say who "those who saw the king's face" were and what mustering was for. Readable splits the list into three sentences.

decisions.choice: eunuch (Literal); court officer (Balanced); palace official (Readable)
decisions.reason: As set for this word in Jeremiah and in 2 Kings 24:12, Literal keeps "eunuch", and Balanced and Readable say "court officer" and "palace official" (m2). 2 Kings 25:19 has "official" and "officer" here; this verse follows the wording set for Jeremiah instead.

records.gloss: And took them Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards, and brought them to [the] king of Babylon to Riblah.
pieces: Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard led them away to Riblah and brought them before the king of Babylon.

L.26: And Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon, to Riblah.

R.26: Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took them all to the king of Babylon at Riblah.

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 25:20
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is the same as 2 Kings 25:20, and the wording follows it.

decisions.choice: Riblah: Nebuchadrezzar's camp in Syria
decisions.reason: As in verse 9, where Zedekiah had been judged.

records.source: וַיַּכֶּ֣ה אוֹתָם֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ בָּבֶ֧ל וַיְמִתֵ֛ם בְּרִבְלָ֖ה בְּאֶ֣רֶץ חֲמָ֑ת וַיִּ֥גֶל יְהוּדָ֖ה מֵעַ֥ל אַדְמָתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And struck them [the] king of Babylon and put them to death at Riblah in [the] land of Hamath. And went into exile Judah from upon its land.
pieces: The king of Babylon had them struck down and executed at Riblah, in the land of Hamath. So Judah went into exile, away from its own land.

L.27: And the king of Babylon struck them and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah went into exile from its land.

R.27: The king of Babylon had them killed there at Riblah, in the land of Hamath. So the people of Judah were taken away from their land as captives.

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 25:21; then the accounts part
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is the same as 2 Kings 25:21. Kings goes on to tell of Gedaliah, the governor left over the land, his murder and the flight to Egypt (2 Kings 25:22-26). Jeremiah leaves that out, having told it at length (40:7-43:7), and gives instead the numbers taken into exile (verses 28-30).

decisions.choice: Judah went into exile from its land
decisions.reason: The same words were said of the northern kingdom (2 Kings 17:23). Jeremiah had warned for forty years that the LORD would send Judah out of the land (1:13-16; 25:8-11).

decisions.choice: the people of Judah (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:21, Readable says "the people of Judah" for the nation, and "as captives" for going into exile.

records.source: זֶ֣ה הָעָ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֶגְלָ֖ה נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֑ר בִּשְׁנַת־שֶׁ֕בַע יְהוּדִ֕ים שְׁלֹ֥שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֖ים וְעֶשְׂרִ֥ים וּשְׁלֹשָֽׁה׃
records.gloss: This [is] the people whom exiled Nebuchadrezzar: in [the] year seven, Judeans three thousand and twenty and three.
pieces: These are the people Nebuchadrezzar carried into exile: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans.

L.28: This [is] the people whom Nebuchadrezzar carried into exile: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans.

R.28: Here are the numbers of people Nebuchadrezzar took away as captives. In the seventh year that he was king, he took 3,023 people from Judah.

decisions.choice: verses 28-30 are part of the Hebrew text; the Greek lacks them
alternatives: leave out verses 28-30 with the Greek
decisions.reason: As far as is known from general knowledge, the Septuagint of Jeremiah does not have verses 28-30 and goes straight from verse 27 to the release of Jehoiachin (verse 31). 2 Kings 25 does not have them either. This translation follows the Hebrew (see the note at 1:1).

decisions.choice: the seventh year: the exile of Jehoiachin in 597 BC, with a smaller number than 2 Kings 24
alternatives: a deportation from the towns of Judah before Jehoiachin's surrender
decisions.reason: Nebuchadrezzar's seventh year is the year he took Jerusalem the first time and carried off King Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:10-16). 2 Kings 24:12 calls it his eighth year, probably counting the year he came to the throne as his first; the two books count his reign in different ways. 2 Kings 24:14 says ten thousand were taken then, and 24:16 seven thousand fighting men and a thousand craftsmen, far more than 3,023. This list may count only the adult men, or only the people of one class or from certain towns, or it may come from a Babylonian record of a particular group. What it counted is not known.

decisions.choice: Judeans: people of Judah
decisions.reason: The word names the people of the kingdom of Judah, as in 32:12 and 40:11-12.

decisions.choice: this is the people: a list follows
decisions.reason: The words introduce the three numbers that follow in verses 28-30 and their total.

decisions.choice: the seventh year that he was king; he took (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says whose years are counted and repeats the verb so that each number is a full sentence.

records.source: בִּשְׁנַ֛ת שְׁמוֹנֶ֥ה עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה לִנְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֑ר מִיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם נֶ֕פֶשׁ שְׁמֹנֶ֥ה מֵא֖וֹת שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וּשְׁנָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: In [the] year eight-teen of Nebuchadrezzar, from Jerusalem, person[s] eight hundred thirty and two.
pieces: In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar, 832 people from Jerusalem.

L.29: In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar, from Jerusalem, 832 persons.

R.29: In Nebuchadrezzar's eighteenth year, he took 832 people from Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the eighteenth year: the fall of Jerusalem, 587 or 586 BC
decisions.reason: This is the year Jerusalem fell and the temple was burned. Verse 12 and 2 Kings 25:8 date those events to Nebuchadrezzar's nineteenth year. The list here seems to count his reign the way verse 28 does, a year lower than Kings; see the note there.

decisions.choice: 832 from Jerusalem: a small number for the fall of the city
decisions.reason: After a siege of a year and a half, with famine and fighting, few may have been left to take. The number may also count only the leading men or the heads of families, as verse 28 may. The text does not say.

decisions.choice: persons: literally "souls"
decisions.reason: The word counts individual people, as in Genesis 46:27.

decisions.choice: he took (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 28.

records.source: בִּשְׁנַ֨ת שָׁלֹ֣שׁ וְעֶשְׂרִים֮ לִנְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּר֒ הֶגְלָ֗ה נְבֽוּזַרְאֲדָן֙ רַב־טַבָּחִ֔ים יְהוּדִ֕ים נֶ֕פֶשׁ שְׁבַ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת אַרְבָּעִ֣ים וַחֲמִשָּׁ֑ה כָּל־נֶ֕פֶשׁ אַרְבַּ֥עַת אֲלָפִ֖ים וְשֵׁ֥שׁ מֵאֽוֹת׃פ
records.gloss: In [the] year three and twenty of Nebuchadrezzar exiled Nebuzaradan chief of [the] guards [of the] Judeans person[s] seven hundred forty and five; all [the] persons [were] four thousand and six hundred.
pieces: In the twenty-third year of Nebuchadrezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile 745 Judeans. In all there were 4,600 people.

L.30: In the twenty-third year of Nebuchadrezzar, Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard carried into exile of the Judeans 745 persons; all the persons [were] 4,600.

R.30: In Nebuchadrezzar's twenty-third year, Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took away 745 more people from Judah. Altogether 4,600 people were taken.

decisions.choice: the twenty-third year: a third deportation, about 582 BC
decisions.reason: No other passage tells of this deportation, five years after the fall of Jerusalem. It may have been a punishment after the murder of Gedaliah and the Babylonian soldiers at Mizpah (41:1-3), or part of a later campaign in the region; the Jewish historian Josephus speaks of a campaign against Ammon and Moab in Nebuchadrezzar's twenty-third year. This is stated from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: all the persons: the total of the three lists
decisions.reason: The three numbers add up exactly: 3,023 and 832 and 745 make 4,600.

decisions.choice: Nebuzaradan again
decisions.reason: The same officer who burned the city and led the second exile (verses 12-16) leads the third.

decisions.choice: more; were taken (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable adds "more" to show that this group is added to the others, and "were taken" to complete the total.

records.source: וַיְהִי֩ בִשְׁלֹשִׁ֨ים וָשֶׁ֜בַע שָׁנָ֗ה לְגָלוּת֙ יְהוֹיָכִ֣ן מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֔ה בִּשְׁנֵ֤ים עָשָׂר֙ חֹ֔דֶשׁ בְּעֶשְׂרִ֥ים וַחֲמִשָּׁ֖ה לַחֹ֑דֶשׁ נָשָׂ֡א אֱוִ֣יל מְרֹדַךְ֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ בָּבֶ֜ל בִּשְׁנַ֣ת מַלְכֻת֗וֹ אֶת־רֹאשׁ֙ יְהוֹיָכִ֣ין מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֔ה וַיֹּצֵ֥א אוֹת֖וֹ מִבֵּ֥ית הַכְּלֽוּא׃
records.gloss: And it was in [the] thirty and seven year of [the] exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in [the] twelfth month, on [the] twenty and five of the month, lifted Evil-Merodach king of Babylon, in [the] year of his reign, [the] head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and brought him out from [the] house of the imprisonment.
pieces: In the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin king of Judah went into exile, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, Evil-Merodach king of Babylon, in the year he became king, showed favor to Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison.

L.31: And it came about in the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth [day] of the month, [that] Evil-Merodach king of Babylon, in the year of his reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out from the house of imprisonment.

R.31: Jehoiachin king of Judah had been in exile for thirty-seven years. Then Evil-Merodach became king of Babylon. In the year he became king, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, he showed Jehoiachin favor and brought him out of prison.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:27: the twenty-seventh day
decisions.reason: The verse follows 2 Kings 25:27, but Kings dates the release to the twenty-seventh of the month, not the twenty-fifth. The difference may come from copying, or from counting the order and the release separately. Jeremiah also adds "and brought him out", where Kings has only "from the house of imprisonment".

decisions.choice: lifted up the head: showed favor and released
decisions.reason: To lift up someone's head is to raise him from disgrace to favor, as Pharaoh lifted up the head of his cupbearer and brought him out of prison (Genesis 40:13, 20).

decisions.choice: Evil-Merodach: the Babylonian king Awel-Marduk
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:27, the name is the Hebrew form of Awel-Marduk, "man of Marduk", Nebuchadrezzar's son, who reigned for about two years. In Hebrew the first part sounds like the word for "foolish", which may be no more than the way the name was heard.

decisions.choice: Jehoiachin: the king Jeremiah also calls Jeconiah and Coniah
decisions.reason: The verse uses the form Jehoiachin, as Kings does. Elsewhere Jeremiah calls the same king Jeconiah (24:1; 27:20) and Coniah (22:24, 28), and said that no son of his would sit on David's throne (22:30).

decisions.choice: the thirty-seventh year: about 561 BC
decisions.reason: Jehoiachin was taken to Babylon at eighteen, in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8-15). Thirty-seven years later, in the year Evil-Merodach came to the throne, he was about fifty-five. The twelfth month falls at the end of winter.

decisions.choice: showed favor ... and brought him out (Balanced); showed Jehoiachin favor (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:27, Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom instead of the picture of lifting the head, and say "in the year he became king" for "in the year of his reign". Readable splits the date into short sentences. Balanced says "the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin ... went into exile" for "the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin".

records.heading: Kindness to Jehoiachin

records.source: וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ טֹב֑וֹת וַיִּתֵּן֙ אֶת־כִּסְא֔וֹ מִמַּ֗עַל לְכִסֵּ֧א הַמְּלָכִ֛ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ בְּבָבֶֽל׃
records.gloss: And he spoke with him good things, and set his seat above [the] seat of the kings who [were] with him in Babylon.
pieces: He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honor above the seats of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.

L.32: And he spoke good things with him and set his seat above the seat of the kings who [were] with him in Babylon.

R.32: He spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and gave him a place of honor, higher than that of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 25:28
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as 2 Kings 25:28 apart from the form of the word "above", and the wording follows it.

decisions.choice: spoke good things with him: spoke kindly to him
decisions.reason: To speak "good things" is to speak kindly and favorably (12:6), perhaps also promising him good treatment.

decisions.choice: the seat above the other kings: first place among the captive kings
decisions.reason: The Babylonian kings kept rulers of conquered lands at their court. Jehoiachin was given a seat higher than all of them, a public sign of honor.

decisions.choice: a seat of honor; a place of honor (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:28, Balanced and Readable say what setting his seat above the others meant, and add "other" for the kings.

records.source: וְשִׁנָּ֕ה אֵ֖ת בִּגְדֵ֣י כִלְא֑וֹ וְאָכַ֨ל לֶ֧חֶם לְפָנָ֛יו תָּמִ֖יד כָּל־יְמֵ֥י חַיָּֽו׃
records.gloss: And he changed [the] clothes of his imprisonment, and he ate bread before him continually all [the] days of his life.
pieces: So Jehoiachin put off his prison clothes, and for the rest of his life he ate regularly at the king's table.

L.33: And he changed his prison clothes, and he ate bread continually before him all the days of his life.

R.33: Jehoiachin no longer had to wear prison clothes. For the rest of his life he ate his meals at the king's table.

decisions.choice: the same words as 2 Kings 25:29
decisions.reason: The verse is the same as 2 Kings 25:29 with "continually" and "before him" in the other order, and the wording follows it.

decisions.choice: he changed: Jehoiachin changed his clothes
decisions.reason: The subject is most likely Jehoiachin, who put off his prison clothes; it could also be the king, who had them changed. Either way his time as a prisoner was over.

decisions.choice: ate bread before him: ate at the king's table
decisions.reason: To eat at the king's table was a mark of honor and of provision for life, as David gave Jonathan's son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:7, 13).

decisions.choice: Jehoiachin; at the king's table (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:29, Balanced and Readable name Jehoiachin and say "at the king's table" for "before him".

records.source: וַאֲרֻחָת֗וֹ אֲרֻחַת֩ תָּמִ֨יד נִתְּנָה־לּ֜וֹ מֵאֵ֧ת מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֛ל דְּבַר־י֥וֹם בְּיוֹמ֖וֹ עַד־י֣וֹם מוֹת֑וֹ כֹּ֖ל יְמֵ֥י חַיָּֽיו׃
records.gloss: And his allowance, an allowance continual, was given to him from with [the] king of Babylon, [a] matter of [a] day in its day, until [the] day of his death, all [the] days of his life.
pieces: And the king of Babylon gave him a regular allowance, a portion for each day, until the day he died, all the days of his life.

L.34: And his allowance, a regular allowance, was given to him by the king of Babylon, a day's portion each day, until the day of his death, all the days of his life.

R.34: Every day the king of Babylon gave him what he needed for that day. This went on as long as he lived, until the day he died.

decisions.choice: 2 Kings 25:30 with "until the day of his death"
decisions.reason: The verse follows 2 Kings 25:30, but names "the king of Babylon" where Kings has "the king", and adds "until the day of his death". The same words closed the account of Zedekiah (verse 11): both kings of Judah ended their days in Babylon, one blind in prison, the other honored at the king's table.

decisions.choice: a day's portion each day: a daily share
decisions.reason: The phrase is used of a daily quota or ration (Exodus 5:13; 16:4). The king provided for him day by day.

decisions.choice: the allowance: royal rations
decisions.reason: Clay tablets from Nebuchadrezzar's palace in Babylon record rations of oil given to "Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahud" and to his sons, which shows that Jehoiachin was already supplied by the court years earlier.

decisions.choice: an open ending: the book closes with David's heir alive in exile
decisions.reason: The book of Jeremiah does not end with the burning of the temple but with the king of David's line freed and honored in Babylon. Jeremiah had told the exiles to settle there and wait, for the LORD would bring them back after seventy years (29:4-14). The writer does not say what Jehoiachin's release means, but the ending leaves room for the hope the book has held out (23:5-6; 33:14-17).

decisions.choice: the king of Babylon gave him (Balanced, Readable); what he needed for that day (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 2 Kings 25:30, Balanced and Readable make the king the subject instead of the passive "was given". Readable explains the allowance and puts "as long as he lived" before "until the day he died" so that the two phrases do not repeat each other word for word.
